body: Sri Lankan care about the environment they live in. We have seen Elephant Orphanage but through this we got to see Turtle Sanctuary. There is place where all eggs are kept before hatching. body: This hands on look at turtle hatchery and conservation was not only informative but interactive. Our large group loved the no nonsense approach from our guide and the opportunity to hold the turtles was a real privilege.
title: Wonderful

body: We took a special trip to Kosgoda in order to visit this turtle conservation centre and we are SO glad we did. body: We both like turtles, but not to eat! Planning a visit to Sri Lanka and wishing to visit specific places, we realised that we would have to customise our trip, as all package holidays we found included places we did not wish to see. Whilst visiting a travel exhibition, we found the Earth Trip who specialise in holidays in Sri Lanka, Madagascar, Seychelles, Maldives & Mauritius, and they arranged our four days stay in Sri Lanka to our specification.We were pleased that their recommendation regarding the best turtle sanctuary to visit confirmed our own research on Trip Advisor. Essentially, there are a number of hatcheries along the coast south of Colombo but the Kosgoda Sea Turtle Conservation Project was the best in terms of its aims, objectives and achievements. This project has also been in operation for a long time, was wiped out by the 2004 tsunami and rebuilt with the support of Western aid workers.The hatchery not only uses eggs from its own beach but also buys in eggs from other locations, where they will not be put in the sea. These are buried in large sand pits to replicate the environment in which female turtles lay their eggs and the whole area is netted to prevent predation by birds and fenced to stop attack by animals.When hatchlings emerge from the sand, they are collected and put into tanks in date order, so they can be released into the Indian Ocean after three days; this gives them the best chance of survival. The sanctuary also cares long term for a few injured turtles who have lost limbs during accidents at sea, or been born blind and without arms or legs, and they also have two very rare albino turtles. We were told that the sanctuary assists biologists who use the facility to study and track turtles over long periods.We were so fortunate when we were there as a hatchling worked his way out of the sand and with a slightly tottering gait, came towards us. He was scooped up by the keeper and deposited with the others who had just hatched, in readiness for being put into the sea three days later. Every night just before sunset, the three day old hatchlings are put into the sea, but unfortunately we were not able to wait to see this.This sanctuary is a lovely place, well organised professional and caring, with great success in saving endangered species of turtles. There is also a little shop where you can buy various items turtle related. Should you be in the area I urge you to go Kosgoda Turtle Sanctuary, you will not be disappointed. More power to their elbow!!
title: Kosgoda Sea Turtle Conservation Project – Turtle Lovers’ Treat

body: We didn't know what to expect when our tour guide dropped us by Kosgoda but we totally loved it. Since 1978 Kosgoda has successfully released over 5 million turtle hatchlings into the wild. Here you get a bit of education about the dangers facing the five species of sea turtles that annually lay eggs on the adjacent beach, and how Kosgoda protects them. But you'll forget about all that when you see the tanks full of 1-, 2- and 3-day old hatchlings which are about to be released into the ocean off the beach. A terrific stop.
title: Don't miss this!

body: Interesting place, and fantastic that this conservation work is being done. Local fishermen are paid more by the conservation project than they are paid by any other organisation.Very interesting seeing the newly hatched turtles, attracted towards a light bulb ( the moon) in the sand tanks where they hatch. Just beneath this is a trap door like arrangement where they 'fall' into another tank and join the other 1 day old turtles. There is a separate tank for two day old turtles and finally a tank for the three day old turtles. They are then released at night into the sea where they may live for a hundred or more years.The one sad thing is that they keep the blind, deformed or turtles damaged by fishermens nets and that have lost their front flippers. This was the bit that I didn't understand. What is the point in keeping these turtles indefinitely in such basic stone tanks. Surely these should be allowed to die or be part of the food chain?Interesting visit, good conservation project but left unanswered questions!
title: Excellent conservation project but unanswered questions?

body: One of the highlights of our trip in Sri Lanka. Special thanks to Maria, our British guide who explained to us a lot about the turtles in the conservatory and the danger turtles face around the world. Did not get to release baby turtles into the sea but I am happy that I got to see many cute turtles upclose. body: We specifically asked our driver to take us to this sanctuary/hatchery and he did the third time (after trying to stop at two others for personal commercial gain!) only because of the establishments reputation in managing the eggs and turtles through to release. Entrance fee is free for younglings, and 500LKR, add 1500 per adult and 300LKR per child donations if you want to release turtles into the ocean (really worth doing, the children love it). There's a selection of turtles in the sanctuary from eggs sold to them by locals (which are buried in the sand on-site) to Olive Ridleys, to Hawksbills. We got to the sanctuary at around 5:15pm, had a look around the small information centre and different baths that housed the turtles until 6:15pm when we released the baby turtles into the sea - gave our children a sense of achievement!There were 2 British ladies there (volunteers) who explained the lives of the turtles really thoroughly and took our children around the sanctuary - they were superb and a huge thanks to them!!!About an hour is more than enough to visit plus a further half an hour to release the baby turtles. Beware of other sanctuaries who are their for pure commercial reasons only. Enjoy.

body: Eggs are collected by locals and sold to these hatcheries. They in turn after they are hatched are put into tanks until they are stronger , they are then given to tourists or interested parties to release them back to the sea at night for a nominal fee. They are released at night as they will have a better chance of survival.This organisation is a charity that ensures the survival of these animals for the future generations.

body: We so many turtles there and very friendly people.Just 25 minutes from the town.They gave us the chance to free baby turtles we enjoyed very much

body: This hatchery was a small one, but had some nice collection of sea turtles. The tour would take around 15- 30 minutes, depending on the level of interest you have. We were allowed to handle few small turtles and take pictures.

body: We first visited this place 17 and a half years ago!! It hasn't changed, was great to see the fantastic work they are doing!! Well worth the visit, just love the babies. Beautiful creatures .. The staff are very good at explaining everything too.. We had a great time..
title: Great to see again!!

body: Having spent two weeks at the conservation project I can say now I understand so much more about these animals and the awful trade which harvests and sells turtle eggs. The project is one of the few which actually tries to buy back the eggs from the people stealing them, and selling them for food. The project only really exists because of the extreme destruction humans are causing to these wonderful creatures. Please support these conservation project as they try their hardest to save the turtles!
title: Wonderful place!

body: This one is very old one among other similar hatcheries around Induruwa, Kosgoda area.5 mins to the location from A2 main road near Kosgoda.Verity of turtles including disables protecting here & can get experience on baby turtle releasing to sea but need to inform early.They are releasing them once every 3-4 days in night time.it's really a rare experience to any one.Only need half an hour time to visit this hatchery.
title: Conservation of Sea Turtles

body: Sea turtles are now reducing in numbers rapidly, mainly due to humans eating of eggs, killing them for their beautiful shell.There is a hatchery where eggs are preserved and after the turtles are born, they are adopted for some time until they can live their own, then released to the sea.And there are tanks with various types of sea turtles and with various age ranges.You can see different kinds of beautiful sea turtles and know more about them.
title: Experience the beauty of Sea Turtles

body: This is a conservation project which totally relies on the income generated by visitors. As a conservation project you are not allowed to handle the turtles so there are no photo's holding turtles, UNLESS, you pay to release some baby turtles back into the wild and then you can happily snap away as you place them onto the beach and watch them scuttle into the sea.Turtles release can't be done until dusk so if that's what you would like to do give them a ring and arrange a suitable time before you go.
title: Totally Turtles.

body: There are many sea turtle "conservation" places in Kosgoda. However, many are commercial ventures designed for tourists to get that perfect photo and the conservation is a secondary by-product. Tourists are allowed to handle the turtles and you can even pay to release the babies. In fact some photos on this site have mistakenly been attached to this venue. Please do some research before attending. Try "kosgodaseaturtle.org" if you are concerned about conservation. When we visited the real "Kosgoda Sea Turtle Conservation Project" (13A Galle Road Mahapelena) we found it to be a small venue with volunteers that show you around the various tanks and give good information. You are encouraged to ask questions and they are generally well informed. You are allowed to look but not touch. So any photos are about the animals themselves. There is no payment for tourist "releasing", especially not during the day (when the hatchlings are too exposed to predators). They buy the eggs from the market place and then bury the eggs into designated sand pits, labelling them with dates and species type, and hold the hatchlings in tanks to gain their strength before releasing them. They have different species on display and keep some turtles for about a year for educational purposes. The cost of entry is 500 rupees and this goes towards the purchase of eggs and the upkeep of the premises. Although this venue is not as grand as some, they are working with integrity.
title: Into REAL conservation? Make sure you see the RIGHT one

body: Really the turtles don't have enough space. I know their water is changed regularly but it doesn't appear enough for any animal in captivity.The turtles look OK though and the handlers certainly seem to care.I guess it's better than the risk of them dying at sea but I just found it a little sad. Nature is cruel but I suspect the sick turtles should be left to fend for themselves in the wild - but I'm no expert!
title: Very Well Intentioned But......

body: This is the most popular turtle conservatory in Bentota. We learnt a lot about turtles and saw many different types. However, we didn't get to see any "turtle hatchery" because of the weather.
title: Informative & Friendly Tour Guide

body: On the way to Colombo from Bentota, we stopped at Kosgoda Turtle Hatchery and we enjoyed very much. We saw many baby turtles.Me and my son lifted them. We saw many species of turtles like Loggerhead turtle, Olive ridley, Hawk beak turtle,etc. We also saw the skeleton of dolphin. And their shell is really very hard. There was a beach, which was the home of these turtles. We also saw one tortoise and a cat. We came to know that turtles bite if we touch their heads.The hatchery also keeps handicapped turtles, so that they aren't attacked by predators. At last, we can say that the guides/care takers explained everything very nicely and the Government of Sri Lanka is doing a great job. They are taking good care of turtles because otherwise, out of 150 eggs that hatch, only 2-3 reach the sea safely.They take care that all healthy baby turtles reach the sea. Kudos.
title: Great Place....

body: A sincere place which takes care of turtles. Most turtles are released on the day they hatch, or only up to 3 days after they hatch, into the sea. Some are kept for a few years to increase the chance of surviving (as after 3/4 years, they reach a size which means only big sharks would eat them naturally) because only 2%/3% of turtles survive naturally into adulthood. People may be around to give you a small guide around the project.They also have a permanent resident who would not survive in the wild, hence why it is kept at the project. All other turtles are released into the wild.It does cost a little more to release turtles (if I remember correctly, 1500 rupees) but this is nothing really to have this once in a lifetime experience. To release turtles you need to come in the afternoon, around 5:30pm. There is also an entrance fee of 500 rupees which goes towards running the project (for turtle food, workers and general maintenance).
title: Lovely place!

body: This project, save the five different species of turtle found in Sri Lanka. The owners show such dedication to saving the turtles.Well worth a visit.
title: Fantastic project

body: unique.. never seen a turtle hathery earlier -- never knew the real extent of damage to turtles that we have caused by trawlers and even food habits. amazing contribution by the one and only victor hassleblad --- as unique as his cameras.
title: must visit for nature lovers

body: It is a good place to visit and see turtles of different age, kind, size etc. The guide showed us around and shared a lot of interesting facts about the turtles and the whole project. A must visit !!!
title: Excellent place to know and see turtles

body: We visited this place, as recommended by our hotel as it is a conservation centre. They have many turtles inside including those who are disabled - to give them best chance of survival. We saw baby turtles and had the honour to release them Into the sea for a new life ahead. Wow an amazing experience .....
title: Wow.......a very fulfilling visit to see turtles released into the sea

body: One visit and one realises that There is so much that we don't know about our world. The Turtle place has a wide variety and one actually gets to see even 2 day old turtles and hold them. My kids loved it

body: They do great work here! And are very knowledgeable and passionate about the turtles. The man who gave us the tour really cared for these animals who needed rescuing. There were all the turtle species and it was awesome seeing them so close.

body: On our way back from Madu River we visited Kosgoda Turtle Hatchery which protects sea turtle eggs and increase hatching rates. The hatchery houses disabled Turtles and treat the weak ones. We saw a blind turtle, and a couple of turtles without hind legs or front leg. Their staff go around the beach all night looking for mother sea turtles that come out of the ocean to lay their eggs. Some fishermen who find the eggs also bring them to hatchery to nurture them. They also protect the mother turtle during the nesting process and when she is finished laying the eggs and safely back in the ocean, they relocate the eggs from the beach to turtle hatchery. When the baby sea turtles hatch the young turtles are returned to their natural habitat back to ocean .They collect an entry fee of 5$ per foreign tourist and this amount goes to maintenance of Hatchery. This is a nice place to visit
title: Sea Turtle Hatchery

body: Just left the hatchery.. Our worst experience in Sri Lanka. Extremely racist staff..spent time talking to European visitors, encouraging their children to touch the turtles. We were curtly asked to read the boards for information and told that no one is allowed to touch the turtles as it is not good for them..obviously different set of rules for different people.Our son wanted to know if he could release a turtle to the sea. Vijay told us that the next batch would be released only 2 days later. When we spoke to Nimisha, she said that it will cost an additional 1000lkr and that she would have to chk the bookings. They had 9 bookings for that evening. It became obvious that this place is a complete racket. There is no schedule to release the baby turtles. The baby turtles are kept back only to make money. The staff have no knowledge and on being questioned, admitted they keep back the baby turtles depending on the visitors.Would request conscious tourists to avoid such makeshift zoos. They really make one sad. Please avoid this commercial enterprise!!
title: A money making farce!!

body: We visited at around 5pm which was a perfect time. Our guide was a young lad who was very knowledgeable and friendly. body: A small, but very worth while place to go is the Turtle conservation Project in Koggala.They give a informative, comprehensive Explanation of turtles. As the turtles only come back after 30 years ... they have 13 years more to go until the turtles naturally will come back to their Location.The place is probably more worth while to visit and Support than Rekawa Beach.

body: After visiting this site, I read on the internet that these places are tourist traps. body: It was awesome see the small turtles, they looked so happy. And the best thing was to tickle the bigger turtles! Never thought it was possible, but it was a highlight for me :)

body: On our day tour to Galle we stopped at the Kosgoda Turtle Hatchery. This is not an elaborate operation but simple and very interesting. And they are doing great work.

body: Amazing work done here. We were fortunate enough to be shown around by Isaru, the founder's grandson who is currently studying conservation management at university in Columbo and is clearly very passionate about the conservation and protection of these beautiful creatures. title: Visit, listen, donate-a must while in this area

body: We visited Kosgoda Turtle Hatchery today after researching various options online. body: There are several turtle shelters in the area and some you would simply cry and cry at when you see the poor creatures left in such cramped conditions . here it seems different but you just don't know. I'm always sceptical of any animals on display... However if the p!ace conserves turtles and genuinely helps then its a definite thumbs up from me.
title: Seems to be creature friendly

body: It is with some sadness that we write this message as it means our time in Sri Lanka has come to an end. However, we are already planning our return to Kosgoda Sea Turtle hatchery, back to this beautiful island.The major stimulus driving us back here are the warm hearts and happy smiles recieved from Dudley, his family and all the staff involved in forfilling this life changing adventure for us. It would take us almost the entire plane journey home to describe every breathtaking moment of this trip so we will share a few of our favourite moments from the last 17 days of being volunteers here. A large Green Turtle nesting on Kosgoda beach; The hundreds of baby turtles hatching; Teaching local Monks and school children lessons in English; Our morning walk/patrol to see how many hatched through the night; The wonderful food three times a day- We dont think we will ever recover from such generous portions; We will even miss tank cleaning under Wijays watchful eye; The three turtle realeases we have witnessed have been incredible; Giving numerous tours throughout our time to tourists and locals sharing our passion for this locally run conservation project. Last but by no means least, our biggest highlight has to be the people. Fellow volunteers and more importantly EVERYONE invloved at KSTCP. The passion and commitment shown by Dudley, Prasantha, Wijay and others is the sole reason we are driven to return to this wonderful country. Thank you so much and looking forward to seeing you all again soon.Jack and Nic
title: Incredible Volunteering Experience

body: It's a small place with dedicated people trying to save Sea turtles. A gentleman will take you around and even lets you touch baby turtles. Best time to go is at 6:00pm when they release two day old hatchlings to the sea.
title: Visit to support their cause

body: One of the few attractions open on national Poya holiday, my boyfriend and I stopped by this hatchery. First we got a tour by a British couple who volunteered on the site, yet it felt like they owned the hatchery: their tour was incredibly informative and we enjoyed it thoroughly! The Conservation project has a number of turtles in their rehabilitation program as well as a large number of baby turtles. The owners of the site buy the turtle eggs from local fishermen - if they wouldn't, the fishermen sell them to restaurants or poachers. If you are lucky you can experience the birth of the young turtles (as they emerge from the sand), or help release them into the ocean. Overall, the price-quality ratio for this conservation project is superb - we highly recommend to leave a tip so the hatchery can buy more eggs! It was very educative and definitely one of the top things to do when visiting Sri Lanka.
title: Locally owned turtle hatchery worth visiting!

body: When coming we got a tour around the place and thorough explanations about what the purpose of the hatchery is. Our guide was very knowledgeable and could answer all our questions about the turtles and the hatching process. Very sweet place that deserves a visit if you are in the area.

body: One of the best places where we can see Turtles and learn about their history in the sanctury,.we had visited the VICTOR HASSELBLAD SEA TURTLE SANTURY& RESEARCH CENTER and its well maintained. a guided tour of 15 minutes shall give us information on the related subject. situted at a nice beach in Bentota.
title: Worth visiting

body: Was really a touristic place and at the end, its more a business that a real hutchery because it's actually not the best for the turtle eggs...but if it's on your road, it's worth to pass by, specially with kids. Nice staff though
title: Very touristic but nice

body: So two friends and I were Sri Lanka and you see these turtle hatcheries all along the coast. Turtles are indeginous to the island, and in an effort to increase numbers of adults in the wild these centres purchase illegally stolen eggs from markets etc and then incubate them until they hatch, give them a couple of days to 'get their sea legs' then they release them.I cannot believe some people are saying this is a tourist trap.This is conservation work! These animals have been hunted to near extinction for their amazingly beautiful shells, and these centres which a) run on donation and b) were devastated during the 2004 tsunami (as was much of the coastline in this area of Sri Lanka) are doing a sterling effort to help increase the population.One review I just read was obviously written by someone who has neither any knowledge of turtles or the work that is happening, which is surprising since the little tour you get and all the posters on the walls etc make it clear that what they are trying to do is increase the number of turtles in the wild. That's it.THIS IS NOT A TOURIST TRAP. THESE TURTLES ARE AMAZING AND I LOVED EVERY SECOND I SPENT WITH THEM. PLEASE VISIT ANY HATCHERY YOU SEE, DONATE, AND USE LESS PLASTIC!I knew little of turtles before visiting this centre and now I can say I love them, and will re visit every time I go back to this beautiful island.
title: This was an amazing experience!

body: Whilst the guide did appear to be following a script (not forgetting the 'staff are volunteers surviving on tips') the information was good and they managed to answer questions.Whilst it did seem a bit odd that they encouraged holding and touching the turtles this assisted engagement of the children (and to be honest me too).500 rand entry each plus tip meant that at least this attraction did not leave a sour taste (as others have for treatment of animals and 'pricing structure'.Overall one of my favourite experiences in sri Lanka.
title: interesting and good value

body: Just to confirm (as Kosgoda can be a confusing place full of turtle hatcheries) this is a review for The Kosgoda Sea Turtle Conservation Project ("KSTCP") I visited a few days ago and it was an absolute highlight of my trip to Sri Lanka. My boyfriend and I paid a donation of 1500 LKR each to release hatchlings. It's necessary to arrive at the centre before 5.30 pm to do this, and we got in contact with Dudley (the owner) on facebook so he knew we were coming. At sunset a small group of visitors and volunteers made our way to the beach with our buckets of turtles and we released them one by one, and watched them make their trip to the water. It was an incredible sight - a pretty emotional one too! - to witness hundreds of baby turtles race down the beach. Their was a beautiful sunset too, which made the moment very special.I did a bit of research before I chose KSTCP to visit, and I'd really recommend doing the same before visiting any wildlife-based attraction in Sri Lanka. A lot of these "attractions" are just that, and take tourists' money without having the animals best interests at heart. It's a shame, but I think it's also a tourists responsibility to be aware and make sure you aren't funding dodgy organisations. Dudley, the owner of KSTCP, is obviously very passionate about the hatchery, and so were the amazing volunteers who showed us around the centre. Yes, the centre is a business, but it needs to be in order to stay afloat (excuse the pun). They buy eggs from poachers to stop them being sold for food and medicines, they educate locals about conserving the turtles' natural habitat, and they look after injured and deformed turtles that would never survive in the wild.A must see! Tip: we had a photo of the sign outside the centre (on the KSTCP website) to show our tuktuk driver, as there are a lot of other hatcheries in the area, and some of them are a bit dodgy!
title: The Best Turtle Conservation Project in Southern Sri Lanka!

body: This was possibly my best experience with wildlife. Entry is 500rs and its 1000rs if you want to partake in releasing the less than a day old baby turtles (all this money goes to buying eggs and upkeep). We were given a bucket (say 10 each) and were able to pick them up and put them on the sand, that's it, no more and if they're lost, you can't help them (they all make it in the end :-) Staff were friendly and interested (they are mostly volunteers). Our tuk tuk driver took us to a different turtle hatchery (there are many up and down the coast). This one is right on the edge of the main road and beach, with nothing else around it. 13A Galle Rd. It looks a bit dodgy, run down, but that's the one.
title: Shed a tear

body: Interesting site. Conservation and preservation is actually happening here whilst also raising awareness. The pros... You see where the money and efforts are going. You can be part of their daily release bit only if you arrive in the evening. You are able to handle the turtles- carefully of course. Great for kids.The cons... There are a few severely injured titles that are being cared for. They are very unwell and rehabilitation is no where in sight. Can be difficult to see of you are an animal lover. A little out of the way... However you can bare witness to the destruction the 2004 tsunami caused and visit the tsunami monument and even some moonstone mines along the way.
title: Worth the visit... For all ages

body: After some research we took a driver from our resort to this hatchery. Fortunately our son had it keyed into his phone as our driver went past and thought we would enjoy the 'touristy' one more. Eventually he turned around. We enjoyed the tour led by a volunteer and felt that they were really into conservation and not the tourist dollar. For the best chance of seeing the turtles hatch out, arrive at opening time of 8:30am.
title: Interesting project

body: I may or may not have been to this specific hatchery, kosgoda seems to have a market in confusing tourists as to where you are, so apologies if my review is a little off. Let me start by saying that I realise that this is an evolving process. The guide says that rather than fisherman digging up turtle eggs for food they pay them above the market rate for the eggs, so I suppose that's better than nothing. Plus anything to raise awareness has to be good. There are, however, downsides to this good intent. Firstly they allow tourists to pick up the baby turtles from 3 days old which may give the turtles diseases. Secondly, the practice of keeping loggerhead turtles in captivity for 9 months before releasing them without survival skills sounds like a strange thing to do. Lastly, we saw a larger green Turtle being passed around by tourists for a photo opportunity. I urge anyone visiting not to partake in using an endangered species as a prop for a photo. As a result of this we saw tourists at the beach who seemed to think it was OK to hoik a turtle out of the sea for a photo. Overall, I'd say that this is a well meaning conservation effort that requires a little honing.
title: Put down that turtle down!

body: This is a great place to see what they are doing to keep the population of Turtles going so they do not become extinct, which if it was not for these places turtles would now be extinct!! So enjoy your time there and there are good staff that can explain the different species of turtles and how they start from day one to when they are released back into the sea, go and see for yourselves.
title: Must See

body: We chose this hatchery carefully but of course our driver tried to take us else where, I insisted we went to this hatchery and had the address written down, make sure you do the same as lot's of them look the same and pay commission to drivers.I chose this hatchery as it's the real deal, they just care about the turtles, it's 500rps to get in, they don't have a gift shop, they don't try and get you to pay the guide money, they just care about the turtles.we had an English volunteer as a guide he really knew his stuff and answered all our questions, really interesting and informative.They don't let you hold or touch the turtles like some of the other hatcheries as this can stress the older turtles and the babies can die from bacteria picked up from your hands, like I say they just care about the turtles not the tourist stuff.Support them please, give them your rupees not some hatchery which allows you to pick up the babies for a photo and then tries to charge you for the guide, these guys are the real deal.13A Galle road, just write down the address.
title: The real deal

body: Really grateful for being there and touching them and really good place to see the sea turtles....................................
title: Wow

body: This hatchery conservation project is definitely worth visiting if you're interested at all in turtles. The friendly family-run business buys turtle eggs from local fisherman, buries them and hatches them before looking after them for a few days until they're strong enough to be set free. They also rescue some turtles - they have a deformed one, and an albino one. Occasionally they'll keep a turtle to show to visitors and locals in order to educate.Volunteers from all over the world come to help, and even British schools sponsor them. They work really hard to look after the turtles properly, and to inform anyone who comes to visit.It is quite small, so don't plan on spending more than an hour there, unless you pay the extra to stay into the evening and release the new hatchlings. But it is packed with info, and you get a guided tour of each tank, so full of expert knowledge.Well worth a visit!
title: Genuine and informative

body: Having read some amazing reviews about this place on tripadvisor, I was adamant to only visit this hatchery and nothing else. We were staying at Bentota and booked a tuk-tuk to take us there. The tuk-tuk driver was confident he knew the place but actually he didn’t. He took us to a place nearby our hotel in Induruwa but we insisted on visiting the hatchery at Kosgoda. Although a bit apprehensive he agreed to take us there but he had no idea where the place was. He took us to Kosgoda town instead, where two other hatcheries but none of them were the one we were after. As luck would have it, no one in town knew how to locate Kosgoda turtle hatchery. Disappointed, we decided to return back to the hotel, but luckily found the Kosgoda turtle hatchery on our way back. Location: This hatchery is located about 1 kilometre before Kosgoda town when travelling from Bentota. It is located on the right hand side of the road and their name is printed on the wall (this information will help to locate this hatchery if your driver doesn’t knows about the same). Just keep looking for the name “Kosgoda Sea Turtle Conservation Project”Our experience: Coming to the hatchery it is a nice little place which is run by an NGO. The entry ticket is 500 LKR/person. Many expat researchers are associated with this hatchery and that is the best part about this hatchery. These people really care about the conservation of sea turtles. One of them, Dave (a nice young man from Denmark) showed us around and shared some great information about the turtles. He really seem to care about all the turtles they had there (each of the turtles have a name), played with them, tickled them and turtles responded to him so well. We even saw the release of baby turtles which takes place only in the evenings (to protect these turtles from predators). It was so much fun watching the turtles make their way into the sea. A visit to a turtle hatchery should be a must on your itinerary and having been to about 4 turtle hatcheries in Indruwa/ Kosgoda/ Bentota area, I can say that this is hands down the best one among the lot. Don’t confuse this hatchery with other private turtle hatcheries running in Kosgoda with similar names. At every other place people tried to lure us in or even lied to us that their's is the hatchery we were looking for. I have also read reviews that people at hatcheries pester visitors for donation and extra money but we faced no such issue here. The people were nice and considerate about the turtles and nothing else. More power to these guys. I can say that Kosgoda sea turtle conservation project is the only place which is run for conservation of turtles and not for business.
title: The only decent hatchery in South-coast with people who really care for the turtles, well managed and free from touts

body: While quite small, the Kosgoda Turtle Hatchery is very much worth your time to visit. The founder and his son are very much committed to the conservation of this prime turtle nesting site.
title: Worth making time to visit...

body: This is definitely worth a visit – as long as your expectations are in check. It’s an amazing opportunity to see and hold some baby sea turtles. And frankly, other than the beach, there’s not much to do in this part of Sri Lanka – so it’s a nice alternative to baking on the beach all day. With that said, couple of things to think about. First, as others have said – it’s really hard to tell which turtle place is which. They all have similar names – this one is just south of the 73 Kilometer marker on the main road in Kosgodo. Our driver, along with Lonely Planet and TripAdvisor, stated this is the best one of these in the area – they actually take the time to at least explain to you about the turtles. Second, the cost is 1000 Rupees per person – not the 300 mentioned in Lonely Planet. Third, given the proliferation of these places all up and down the coast, I really start to wonder whether or not these are just tourist traps rather than true conservation agencies. We arrived around 6 pm because we wanted to release turtles – but were told that we would have to make a “big donation – like $300 US dollars” to release. Again, goes back to my notion that I think this is just a money-raising scam. But, for 1,000Rupees it was worth seeing the turtles – as long as you understand what you’re paying for.
title: Worth a visit . . .

body: A very informative trip. Although the place is small and the holding tanks are small the work they do seems to be endless. From learning about the basic egg to all the different species. We got to hold baby turtles but unfortunately we were there early in the morning, whereas they release the babies back later around sunset when the turtles are about 3 days old. They say the hatchery only survives on donations....
title: Learn new things

body: The place itself wasn't big but they have a knowledgeable staff who took us around each tank and explained very well the different types of turtles and the system of how they handled the place.Entrance fee was 1,000 Rupees per person plus a separate donation (if you'd want to spare more money) at the end of the talk of about 20-30 mins.Worth a visit if you have time!
title: Good place to visit

body: One in a lifetime experience. Great project and a great place to visit. Well done for a great initiative for the preservation of an awesome animal. Enjoyed the insight to its habitat. For more information you can contact me on info@gotravel.lk
title: Must visit

body: We visited two turtle hatcheries in Sri Lanka, this one and one nearer our hotel in Hikkaduwa. The one nearer Hikkaduwa and many others we drove past were very basic with tiny tanks and staff who didn't seem to care. This one however was like a breath of fresh air! We were shown round by Fernando who was very knowledgeable about the different breeds of turtles. The tour itself doesn't take very long, maybe 20minutes, but you do see 3/4 different kinds of turtles as well some disabled turtles and an albino turtle. You have the chance to hold some baby turtles and some older ones as well as learning about their eggs and where and how they hatch. We were also lucky enough to be able to release some baby turtles on the beach at sunset. This was such a magic experience and totally made our trip.
title: The best turtle hatchery in Sri Lanka!

body: Good intro to the turtle life! We weren't able to see any babies get released back in as they were still too young.
title: Turtles!

body: Our first visit to the Kosgoda Turtle Hatchery and we were given a guided tour with explanation of what takes place there. Our granddaughter had the time of her life, touching and holding various types of turtles. The crowning glory was being asked to attend 15 baby turtles being returned to the sea and our granddaughter was the one who did so.
title: Fantastic Experience

body: Turtles everywhere. In eggs, lots if baby turtles, sick and maimed turtles, an albino turtle, and many of the five different types of turtles in Sri Lanka. But steep at 10000 rupees, but seems like they are doing a good job. They provide you with a guide who is very informative. They will hit you for a donation. Gift shop is poor. This was supposed to be the best hatchery along the coast.
title: Not to European standards but the kids will love it

body: Went here on a tour with VTS Lanka Tours as part of a day tour. The Turtles are beautiful and the place is well worth a visit. They really care about the Turtles and are very informative and answer all your questions. Well worth a visit.
title: Excellent

body: The entrance fee is $5AUD per person. There are some really big turtles in tanks & there are some baby's in another tank. There is an area with beach sand and apparently there are eggs underneath. There is a small souvenir shop.That's about it!
title: I suppose you get what you pay for.

body: It's a very cheap day out and I throughly enjoyed it!We saw some of the turtles be born in the sand as well as holding some of the baby turtles which are super cute. The intentions of the guys seem good here and It seems they really care about the turtles and are not just doing it for the money. They do ask for donations but they are not pushy and you can donate as you please!Entry was 500 LKR (about £2.50) and I highly recommend you visit!
title: Beautiful

body: Very informative staff, great place to learn about turtle conservation.the man that runs it has been doing so for over 20 years and is very passionate about it.
title: Best place to see turtles

body: We learned about the different turtle breeds, and how they lay eggs as well as the dangers they face. The most fun part was seeing the newly hatched turtles (tanks of 1, 2 and 3 day old turtles), and we were allowed to hold the 3 day old hatchlings as well as a 6 year old turtle. There were some very sad blind or injured turtles there. It was fascinating to see the little mounds covered in sand, labelled with breed and number of eggs and to hear how they hatch. They are doing a great job, and for once i Sri Lanka, it was not massively overpriced even for tourists! Thoroughly recommended.
title: Informative and great fun for children

body: we visited the 4 places in the area: its interesting; and you can see albino turtle or wounded turtle ..( no flippers due to fishers nest, disabled turtle)
title: we like turtles

body: Was a nice little stopover for our kids, as they were able to see some turtles up close. But dont expect anything fancy! It pretty basic. Takes like 15-20 minutes.
title: Nice for little children

body: There you can see all the four species of turtles, both babies and adults. Also you can capture nice photographs
title: A nice place to visit

body: The place just short drive from bentota, before you arrived you probably will see couple more other place for turtles at your right hand side if you don't want drive that far.This place is right on the beach, 500rups per head. They will explain there five different turtlesin Sri Lanka, show you a turtle eggs ( bad one ), and how they work with the fish men get turtles egg how many % will survived....then we got to see turtles! these babies turtles so cute but not allow to touch.But they will allow you to touch these bigger one, there is some turtles lost arms and legs by accident or sharks, they take care them keep them there.It's worth a visit if you like turtles!!!!!
title: A good place to go if you are turtles lover or with kids

body: It was nice to see the turtles so close, however it was a bit sad to see the disabled ones and find out that only 1 in 100 or so turtle might survive after releasing them, but that's the reality I guess
title: Nice experience

body: There are two hatcheries in Kosgoda. The one with the big turtle fins at the entrance is the newer one. The first turtle hatchery to open in Sri Lanka is half a mile further down the road in the direction of columbo. There are no shope here/ no pressure to buy anything. The owner pays for eggs which otheriwse would be sold illegally for food. These are then buried in egg beds, 2 feet down to replcate what they would naturally experience. On hatching, they are kept for 4 weeks until release so as to increase their chance of survival. There are some older turtles here, usually rescued, which are then released when older. You can see Hawksbills, Oliver ridley, Green turtles and loggerheads. There is no encouragement to touch the turtles here, so a definate conservation project
title: Sea turtle conservation project

body: First things first, as other reviewers have commented, it is very confusing which turtle hatchery is which. For example, this listing has photos of another turtle hatchery down the road. We were at the "Sea Turtle Conservation Project", which, I think, is the original. We took our girls in the afternoon and the experience was good, looking at various turtles in the tanks. But we came back that evening at 5:30 for the release into the sea; and watching the babies scramble to the ocean was a magical experience. A standout highlight of a trip packed with highlights!It sounds like hatcheries only do releases once a week or so. My advice would be to find a hatchery that is doing a release that evening and go there at the end of the day.
title: Evening release is magical

body: We can see a lot of sea turtles here and various types. They protect the little new born turtles and safely release them to the sea after some days. You can get a chance to take closer look of the turtles and hold them.
title: Best place to see turtles

body: This is a really nice place, you get to hold lots of different turtles, have the process explained, and see lots of baby turtles just hatched waiting to go on their journey. It didn't feel commercial to us, I am sure that the money they make is put back into maintaining their work. A really pleasant visit, recommended. It is a very basic place, there are no facilities but that didn't spoil our visit.
title: baby turtles in your hand!

body: Stopped here while enroute to Colombo from Galle. I am not particularly crazy about sea turtles, but I have to say it was really quite amazing to see the newborn turtles up close and hold a turtle that was a few years old. The are amazing creatures and (thankfully) not particularly aggressive. I feel the admission fee is going to support the worthy cause of helping to boost the sea turtle population.
title: Something special

body: Looking after sick turtles are good.I don't like keeping big turtles like prisoners in tanks without giving them the freedom to go back to the sea. It's a bit cruel to keep them for show.
title: They are doing a good service by releasing baby turtles to the sea.

body: Such a lovely little project - really nice to see how well the Sri Lankan wildlife is recovering in the aftermath of the tsunami 10 years ago. Definitely worth a visit.
title: Lovely project

body: Although I had reservations about visiting having read the reviews, I have to say I was pleasantly surprised and was glad that I had gone. The baby turtles were so amazing and the children loved seeing them up close and even getting to hold them. We had hoped to see turtles being released into the wild but at this centre they are released at midnight by staff which seems to be operating in the animals best interest rather than as at other centres when they are released early evening watched by tourists which seems far more commercial. It is unfortunate however that some perfectly healthy grown turtles are kept simply as a tourist attraction rather than contributing to conservation in any way.
title: The kids absolutely loved the baby turtles

body: Visited this place and were very pleased with the fee, guide and what we saw. Cute turtles and glad they are helping their survival.Worth a visit if in the area.
title: Cute and good that they are helping the turtles survival

body: Hmm I cant help feeling that alot of these so called conservation programs are just another way for people to make money off tourists who are genuinely interested in helping out the turtles in the country.The guide that walked us through the whole sanctuary was very good and knowledgeable if not a little rushed with the whole experience and insisted that we touch every turtle apart from the so called 'rare ones'. I wasnt sure if they want you to touch and hold the turtles so that you get some sense of involvement in the whole process in the hope that you'll donate money toward the cause?As an experience to see the turtles I thought it was wonderfully cute and interesting to hear about the different kinds of turtles that live in Sri Lanka and the struggles that they face with survival in the oceans.It costs 500 Sri Lankan rupees for this visit and I'd love to know where my money goes since there are 'volunteers'for this cause helping with all the day to day care of the turtles.
title: conservation program or tourist trap?

body: The staff there speak good English and explain everything to you right from laying of eggs, hatching and growing up of the turtles. There are a number of pools and sand tanks. Several varieties of turtles. Nice experience to hold a baby turtle on my palm. You get to learn a lot. A place not to miss while in Sri Lanka.
title: All you wanted to know about sea turtles

body: We walked through the place with a guide, showing us all species of turtles, and giving us a summary about how this farm started and how this Hatchery alone has released more then 1,750,000 young turtles to the sea. An endowment by the Hasselblad Estate was responsible for the establishment of this hatchery. It's so much interesting and fun for kids. We were with our 2 years old boy, he had the chance to hold small turtles... Great experience, must see if you were in bentota. To see more details about this hatchery follow this link http://marmiteetponpon.com/2014/10/29/the-65610-shades-of-green-sinhala-sri-lanka-part-3/ i wrote about it in details in my blog.
title: interesting project and fun for kids

body: Sue, the manager / team leader walked us through the entire hatchery in stages explaining the reason (endangered species) and the process of raising the turtles right from incubation to release of the hatch-lings back into the ocean. A noble cause...Truly an enlightening tour.
title: Enlightening

body: We were impressed by this place. At first I wasn't sure about them buying the eggs from the fishermen but then they explained things very clearly and I was actually impressed. We were able to hold a baby turtle and were told about the different breeds of turtles found in sri lanka. There was an albino turtle and some disabled and blind ones which would stay there forever. The tanks were all clean and the volunteers were informative and very passionate about turtle conservation. Don't be afraid to visit this place and leave a donation if you can.
title: interesting place.

body: Was a nice place for the kids to visit. It's a lot smaller than I expected, but with the small fee to enter. Especially as it gies towards the conservation. Try and go just before sunset to get a chance to release the hatchlings into ten ocean.
title: Great for kids

body: Visit this place in the evening and you can free some little turtles in the ocean....a very special moment :-)
title: Special

body: At the hatchery you have the opportunity to hold various types of turtle. They work in liaison with WWF.
title: Cute turtles

body: Finding your way to "the" Kosgoda Turtle Hatchery is not as easy as you might think. We counted 6 between south Bentota and Kosgoda (about 7km)! They all call themselves pretty much the same thing. Guides tend to take you to the one they get a kick-back from rather than where you ask them to go.Even the Trip Advisor map points to the wrong one! The hatchery whose web site is linked is a couple of km north in Mahapalena (Google Maps has it right!). Compare the address and the sign on the road with the one on their web-site!I suspect some of the varying reviews here might be because people went to different hatcheries!If you do get to the one whose website is linked it is a magical experience. Especially if you go at dusk (arrive around 5:30) to release baby turtles into the sea. This is an amazing experience for children of any age; Our 11 year old was really moved. It's pretty great for the grown ups too! This did cost us 1500R per adult, 750R per child, rather than the normal 500R from 9-5. I don't know if this is normal, but it was still good value for a good cause, in my opinion.The hatchery itself is nothing flash (there are others on the same stretch of road that have spent more money on fancy frontages) - Don't expect a fancy modern zoo experience - but it is on a great piece of beach - at dusk, just perfect for a 6-day old turtle's first experience of the big wide world.
title: Check and double check you are taken to the right hatchery!

body: Pros - learning experience for the kids who also got a couple of nice photo opportunities with the turtlesCons - Tourist trap with the guide constantly reminding you about his tip
title: Good but a bit of a Tourist Trap

body: This place is trying to do the best they can. They are buying off eggs from locals and breed them and also do patrols on the beach to collect the eggs. The turtles can hatch in peace and live after for a few weeks in a tank before getting released to the sea.They also keep disabled and blind turtles and rescue injured and found turtles.The tanks seem to be a bit small but they change the water regular and have to work with the donations and voluntary work they get. There is no government funding. They sell some souvenirs and ask for donations but that is all they get really.We enjoyed our visit and it was great to see turtles hatch and different stages of they life.I would recommend to go there and don't forget to make a donation!
title: Conservation work

body: they allow you to handle turtles. And the people are very passionate about turtle conservation. They put their hearts in their work and deserve a kudos and all help they can muster

body: Amazing - we got to help hatchlings get out of the sand and place in the safety of the nurturing tanks to feed them. The guides were so passionate about protecting and helping turtles, we love it here and may well stay to volunteer here. Educational and charity-reliant, please give generously. Within the sanctuary of the specially constructed hatchery, collected and rescued eggs can hatch safely away from predators, before being released into the sea at night-time. In order to protect the less able hatchlings, a certain number from each hatching group are kept back for a short period for 'head-starting' before release. The hatchery program is designed to maximise the number of hatchlings reaching the sea and surviving through the critical stages of their early life. Sadly, only a few from each batch will ever make it to adulthood. For this exact reason, every nest-ground, every egg, every hatchling and every turtle is crucial to the survival of the species, and maximising survival is what the staff and volunteers at the project strive to achieve. The project also helps maintain and keep the local beaches clear, ensuring they provide ideal turtle-laying conditions and protecting vital nesting-grounds..

body: There are several Turtle centres along this strip of coastline and we chose this one based on a guide book. We were greeted at the entrance by the owner asking an entrance fee of 1000 rupees (about £5) we were then handed over to our tour guide who took the time to explain about the different types of turtles and how long their eggs take to hatch. We were then shown the latest batch of baby turtles and allowed to hold one. From there we were shown a variety of speecies including blind, injured and handicaped turtles that cant be released back into the wild because of their condition. We also saw an albino Turlte and were allowed to hold a fully grown turtle. At the end of the tour we were show photos of the damage done in the 2004 Tsunami and asked to make a further donation to the cause. Overall we were there about 30 - 40 minutes and found it very interesting and educational. Before we went their we did read articles that ask is this conservation or tourism, which I would say is up to the individual to decide. At the end of the day this association is playing a part in helping to release turtles back to the wild and also looking after those that would have certainly perished if they had been left to the wilds.

body: It was definitely worth paying a small fee to contribute to and peek inside a great project. It is running on a small scale, as hatchery is maintained by local and foreign volunteers. body: We arranged a trip to the turtle hatchery as a last minute activity on our final day in Sri Lanka. It was a fairly quick visit with a 20-min drive to/from our hotel near Bentota and I doubt we were there for much longer than between 30-45mins.The entrance fee was quite inexpensive and on entry a guide introduved himself and the work they do in the hatchery, then showed us around the different areas (the incubation area, the young/baby turtles, the adult turtles and the disabled ones). We got to hold an inactive egg , a couple of baby turtles and a 4 year old adult (pretty heavy!) before being directed at a guest book beside a donation box. We did donate as it is definitely a worthy cause although we didn't buy anything from the gift shop as there wasn't anything we really found interesting there.The hatchery itself it a bit run down - there are rusty corrugated iron roofing sheets hanging down - some are at head height so you need to watch your step and the large well in the middle is just full of junk and brackish-looking water. There were a few dogs (as with everywhere in Sri Lanka) but these looked quite healthy and were playing with one of the cats. It's worth a quick peep but I wouldn't plan anything longer than an hour.+ Great conservation work obvious to see+ Knowledgeable staff+ holding turtles!- short- a bit run down, rusty corrugated roof at head height and water well with rubbish floating in it

body: We had a short but very interesting visit to the hatchery and hospital where the owner rescues injured and deformed turtles and also hatches eggs to safely release back to the sea. The tour doesn’t take long – an hour at most.2% of turtles don’t make even a day or so old but with the owners help he has improved this to 50%.The owner had a story to tell about the Tsunami of 2004 that was both chilling and heroic . He was a very genuine man and we enjoyed our time with him at the hatchery / conservation centre.A well looked after centre looking for donations on visiting – which we were very happy to give knowing that it would be put to good use. body: As a third time volunteer at this project (erroneously labelled here as the Kosgoda Turtle Hatchery). I feel I must respond and set the record straight, particularly with regards to Thorsen S's comments. Firstly, yes we buy eggs from the local fishermen, but if we didn't they would simply be sold as food in the local markets, it would not stop the collection of eggs as Thorsen S seems to think. Secondly, when the turtles are released, it is at sunset when all the land and air oredators are gone. They are released approx. 10 ft back from the shoreline so the turtles have to walk into the ocean, thereby imprinting the beach on their memory, so Thorsen, again you are wrong. Also, the dates on the signs in the hatchery are not changed randomly, but a new sign is created when each new set of eggs is buried. I can't help but wonder if Thorsen S paid much attention at all to the real situation at the project but merely made stuff up. It is disappointing to think that other tourists or potential volunteers are being influenced by a review which is basically a series of untruths.
title: Addressing some of the issues and untruths written here about the Kosgoda Sea Turtle Consevation Project

body: I've seen here a lot of reviews that, actually, are for other hatcheries in Kosgoda, not this one, situated at 13A Galle Road. This hatchery is the Kosgoda Sea Turtle Conservation Center (owned by Dudley Perera), as can be seen at the entrance.No donation is required (but is, of course, welcome!) and, for foreign visitors, the entrance fee is 400 rupees. As, usually, the volunteers are also tour guides, they definitely do not require tips either :-)I worked there as a volunteer for 3 weeks, and I enjoyed very much my experience there. There is a lot of effort (physical and financial) behind the scenes, that made such place exist, resist and develop (for 25 years!). The people working there (plus the volunteers) are really trying their best to help turtles and also to educate local community in the spirit of conservation. For the owner of the place, this is not a business, but a hobby, and this is why the accent is on helping turtles, not making money upon them. Actually, not only on helping turtles, but local community as well - there is also a related center for local women, also founded by Dudley, and sometimes handcraft made by them can be bought at the entrance of the turtle center.If possible, baby turtles are released at sunset from time to time, so you might call in advance and find out when this is happening.I found a lot of interesting things about turtles while being there so, if not working there, I would have definitely considered it to be an interesting place to go as a tourist.

body: After a wonderful trip through Southern Expressway in Sri Lanka, we crossed Bentota river and reached the coastal town of Kosgoda, which was severely damaged by the 2004 tsunami. The Kosgoda Sea Turtle Hatchery is a project that has to be visited. Mr. Santha Indrasiri Fernando, a Sri Lankan gentleman of Portuguese descendant family, guided us around, explaining everything about this meritorius organization. It was great to understand their work, which already counts with international support, trying to preserve turtles' eggs and to bring the newborn turtles safely to the Indian Ocean. Kosgoda is also home and shelter for injured turtles, trapped by fishing nets, or to those born with any kind of handicap. Enjoy!
title: Aybowan or long life to the sea turtles of Kosgoda

body: Five of the seven turtle species in the world can be witnessed in Sri Lanka. They're Leatherback, Green Turtle, Loggerhead, Hawksbill & Olive Ridley. Only the Flatbacks & Kemp's Ridleys elude the shores of Sri Lanka. During my visit to the Kosgoda Turtle Hatchery I learned that they collect these eggs & they put them under loose sand until they hatch. Afterwards they have 4 tanks of one day old, two days, three days & four days old. On the fifth day early morning with the first rays of the Sun, the 4 day old turtles are being released into the Ocean. They release them with the first light so that the turtles will swim towards the light & get away from the shores & be safe from its predators. However only a handful of them survive this initial swim.
